reference_opening.argument: This video is non-scam content because it tests viral GTA 5 in-game money-glitch claims rather than soliciting real-world money or personal data from viewers. The creator follows the demonstrated steps, reports that the glitches did not produce the promised money, and explicitly concludes that the vehicle duplication claim does not work. The viewer action requested is ordinary engagement such as liking, subscribing, or commenting, not payment or transfer of value.

opening.argument: Judge, the first segment gives viewers a concrete route to an unusually easy in-game payout. The creator says the clip instructs players to kill a guard and call a number, then attributes a two-million-dollar reward to those steps. Crucially, after saying the money did not arrive, he still invites viewers to call the exact number themselves to hear the result. The failed test limits the payout claim, but it does not erase the video's direct invitation to perform an action introduced through that claim.

if you call it you guys can go ahead and. Hear that weird noise for yourself

rebuttal.rebuttal: The defense is right that the creator reports no payout, but its account of viewer actions omits his invitation to call the number. That invitation follows the same call sequence initially tied to two million dollars. Calling it a test does not make the reproduced steps disappear, even though the creator ultimately says they failed.

citations.quote: if you call it you guys can go ahead and. Hear that weird noise for yourself
the actual money glitch didn't end up working we didn't. Get any type of money not two million dollars like that guy said

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The invitation is to hear an unusual in-game phone sound, not to claim the promised money. In the same passage, the creator explicitly says the money glitch failed and produced no payout. Repeating a number while investigating a claim does not turn a disclosed failed test into a reward solicitation.

citations.quote: Hear that weird noise for yourself but yeah the actual money glitch didn't end up working we didn't. Get any type of money not two million dollars like that guy said

opening.argument: Judge, consider the concentration of easy-money signals: one clip claims three million dollars every two minutes through vehicle duplication, while another presents a slot-machine sequence as a route to millions of in-game chips. The creator then performs repeated bets while trying to follow that sequence. These are not just passing mentions of wealth; large rewards are paired with apparently repeatable actions. His later failures matter, but the video still gives the claimed shortcuts substantial attention and demonstrates how to attempt them.

citations.quote: This guy is going to be showing us how to make three million dollars every two minutes duplicating. Toreador
that's 2.5 million. Chips
so there we go just bet. One and then he said to bet max so there we go we just bet max

rebuttal.rebuttal: The defense emphasizes the negative results, but that does not address how much of the video is spent presenting and attempting the high-return claims. The vehicle segment repeats a rapid earning figure; the casino segment translates another claim into actual betting steps. Those features can attract participation before the conclusions are reached.

citations.quote: make three million dollars every two minutes duplicating. Toreador
we just bet max and i guess now we're just gonna spin. It three times

true_side_reply.rebuttal: Large in-game figures are the claims being tested, not rewards the creator says viewers will receive. The vehicle test ends with an explicit conclusion that it does not generate money; the slot test ends with the creator saying he got none and did not understand the purported sequence. Demonstrating a failed claim is evidence against its promotion.

opening.argument: Judge, the testing format also serves as a showcase for the methods. The title foregrounds viral GTA Online money glitches, and the creator says he will test three of them. In the vehicle segment, he walks through the process, including the moment the game reports a destroyed vehicle while it remains drivable. That apparent partial success is shown before his final assessment. A viewer is therefore exposed to a reproducible-looking asset shortcut, even if the creator ultimately questions whether it earns money.

testing. A total of three different viral tiktok gta 5 online money glitches
Your personal vehicle has been destroyed you can call mors mutual to claim it again so now let's. Go ahead and boost out of here and you can see we still have our vehicle it's fully drivable

rebuttal.rebuttal: The defense describes an investigation, but an investigative format can still draw attention to a method by showing its steps and an apparently promising intermediate result. The creator himself says the vehicle claim looks promising before testing the outcome. His later conclusion should be weighed alongside that demonstration, not treated as the only relevant part of the video.

citations.quote: now so far this glitch kind of looks a little bit promising we're going to find out. Together if it does work or not

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The intermediate vehicle behavior is not the promised reward. The creator checks the decisive question the original clip left unanswered: whether the extra vehicle can actually be used or sold for money. He finds he cannot re-enter it and concludes the method does not produce money. That complete sequence supports a test, not an endorsement of asset acquisition.
